***

**1996**

**I.** 
Here, in our forsaken home on the mesa, the desert breaks into the sweeping curves of mountain territory—a domain defined by the anthropology of the outlaw. It was here that you taught me to shoot that .22 rifle with precision, its stock steadied firmly against my shoulder socket like a wild, pulsing third arm. Together, we practiced the postures of stillness and reserve, adopting the calculated cunning of the predator. In the end, all that remained were shattered bottles scattered among the cowering piñón trees. Here, the natives have never been safe.

**II.** 
You were a curious, sentimental boy intent on the romance of an expedition; I was a clever, cynical woman consumed by the Romantic trope—*mi cielo, mi mar, mi luna, mi tierra*—the cadence of Spanish occupation. Like diligent engineers, we divided the terrain and entered, mapping it for future journeys. The desk lay cluttered with marked sheets, pencil shavings, graphs, incomplete stanzas, and the metaphors and equations of isolated fixed points. In the end, like Malinches, we were left harboring the scattered remnants of one another’s labor.

**III.** 
*La migra:* your mind was skilled at expulsion and vigilant surveillance. Yet, while you policed the perimeter, it was those refused entry—those forced to settle elsewhere—who captivated me. Ours was always a patrolled encounter. My mind, conversely, was what fascinated you: the creases of my cerebrum and the electric streams coursing through its fissures, a landscape ripe for your excavation. You proved yourself a brother to Queen Isabella in your devices, commands, relentless agendas, and missionary schemes; and like the others, you would ultimately insist on exile. 

Yet, I am no Circe. I claim no magical powers, nor am I a victim of this narrative. I am simply a woman with these few words—a woman who has peered through the barrel of a loaded gun, leaving nothing intact.

It was here, in a territory where native peoples have long been denied the basic right to safety, that I first learned to hold and fire a rifle. The heat, the silence, and the weight of iron in my hands bonded the mechanics of survival to a land already haunted by forced subjection.

Over time, our intimacy mutated, adopting the cold logistics of border enforcement and colonial occupation. Our dynamic became entirely panoptic, defined by patrolled perimeters, constant surveillance, and an atmosphere of institutional suspicion. My companion slipped seamlessly into a controlling, missionary-like persona—cloaking absolute authority in the language of righteous intent. He assumed the role of both judge and sovereign, insisting on my exile as if banishment were a necessary act of salvation.

Yet I reject the passive role assigned to me in his narrative. I refuse to be written as a helpless victim of his crusade, nor will I allow myself to be flattened into some tragic, mythic trope of the displaced woman. My agency remains intact, carved out of the very dirt and iron that surrounded us. To hold a loaded weapon, to feel its cold potential and understand its leverage, irreversibly alters the person behind the sight. I am not a casualty of this desert or his doctrine; I am a woman reshaped by the physical reality of power, standing fully transformed in a landscape I now claim on my own terms.

### I. The Grid and the Flesh

The desert was never empty; it was merely rendered legible. 

Long before the watchtowers cast their long, geometric shadows across the salt flats, men in sweat-stained linen unfolded paper across the hood of a truck. They laid down brass dividers and sight-lines, pinning the shifting dunes to a grid of northerning and easting. They called this order. They called this light. 

I learned the geography of my own body through that same arithmetic. You ran a calloused thumb along the ridge of my collarbone as if tracing a contour line on a topo map, measuring the gradient of my surrender. *Terra nullius,* you whispered into the hollow of my throat—a blank space waiting to be named, claimed, and settled. In the sweltering heat of the borderlands, intimacy became an act of occupation. Every touch carried the cold weight of a land grant; every sigh was a treaty signed in dark, evaporative ink. 

To be loved by an empire is to be mapped until there is nowhere left to hide. The state sits on the horizon like a thermal lens, reducing our tangled limbs to heat signatures—crimson, yellow, blue—isolated against the cool, dead expanse of the night.

---

### II. Parallax and Windage

You taught me how to look through a reticle. 

"Account for the wind," you said, your breath warm against my ear as my shoulder absorbed the steel coldness of the stock. "Account for the curvature of the earth. At six hundred yards, the world bends away from you. You have to aim higher than what you want to hit."

The optics of surveillance and the optics of marksmanship share a single, predatory eye. Through the crosshairs, the desert loses its breath. The mesquite bushes freeze; the jackrabbits turn to statues; the migrants moving through the wash become slow-moving vectors, targets waiting for correction. In the logic of the tower, to see is to possess, and to possess is to hold the power of erasure.

You thought you were teaching me submission—how to hold my breath between heartbeats, how to make myself still, how to accept the recoil. You believed that by initiating me into the violence of the border, I would become its ornament: the quiet woman at the edge of the camp, keeping the rifles clean, romanticizing the brutal necessity of the line. 

You forgot that a scope works both ways. The lens that magnifies the target also brings the marksman into terrifying focus.

---

### III. The Memory of Salt

I remember the desert before it was a cage. I remember when the river was not a barrier enforced by razor wire and underwater sensors, but a muddy vein that we crossed with our clothes held high above our heads, laughing at the cold. 

Memory, under the regime of the map, is an illegal act. The state demands a static present—a permanent, immovable fence dividing the civil from the wild, the citizen from the ghost. They paint the desert as a place of natural tragedy, a wasteland that swallows the desperate, hiding the truth that the desert was weaponized by design. The sun is pushed into service as an executioner; the terrain is curated to kill.

In your arms, I pretended to forget the old names of the wells. I let you rewrite my lineage as a series of fortunate rescues. *Look how safe you are here,* your touch implied, *behind the perimeter.* You constructed a myth of my fragile, tragic beauty—the native daughter plucked from the dust, redeemed by the order of the fort.

It was a beautiful story. It was an imperial story. It required me to die at the end, or at least to fade quietly into the dry scrub, a melancholy ghost haunting the border of your grand adventure.

---

### IV. The Reversal

I am burning the maps.

The paper curls in the heat, the red highways turning to black ash, the neat grids buckling into smoke. Latitude means nothing to the dust storm. Longitude cannot stop the flash flood.

I took the rifle from the rack while you slept, the brass casing tasting of copper and salt on my tongue. I did not run into the night as an exile. I did not crawl away into the brush to weep for what was lost. Exile is a category invented by men who think they own the horizon. You cannot banish a woman from the land that birthed her; you can only lose your grip on her.

I walked up to the high ridge, where the wind smells of creosote and ozone. I set the bipod into the dirt. I dialed the elevation. 

Through the clear glass of the reticle, I watched the spotlights of the sector station sweep rhythmically across the fence line. I saw the geometric elegance of your carefully constructed world—the floodlights, the cameras, the chain-link, the iron gates. How fragile it looks when viewed through a quarter-inch of tempered glass. How easily a single lead projectile disrupts the delicate alignment of a optic system.

---

### V. Unmaking the Line

I am not your tragedy. I am not the tragic horizon upon which you test your manhood, nor am I the wilderness you were born to tame. 

When the shot echoes across the canyon, it will not be a cry for help. It will be a structural failure. The glass of the surveillance camera will shatter into a thousand glittering stars, blinding the monitor rooms three miles away. The light will die. The dark will rush back in—wild, unmapped, and sovereign.

You built an empire on the illusion that you were the hunter and the desert was your prize. But you taught me windage. You taught me parallax. You taught me how to adjust for the curvature of a world that refuses to lie flat for you.

Now, the desert belongs to the night again, and the night belongs to me.

In the vast, dramatic landscape of world history, few legends burn with as much tragic intensity as that of La Malinche. Hers is a story positioned at the exact intersection of power, language, and passion—a narrative that has, over the centuries, been reshaped through a deeply **Romantic** lens within the **Spanish**-speaking world and beyond.

When the Spanish fleet arrived on the shores of Mesoamerica in the 16th century, they brought with them a world of iron, faith, and conquest. Yet, the true catalyst of this momentous cultural collision was not merely sword and gunpowder, but speech. Malintzin—known to history as La Malinche or Doña Marina—became the indispensable interpreter, advisor, and companion to the Spanish commander Hernán Cortés. In the clash between the Aztec Empire and the Spanish Crown, she was the bridge, translating not just words, but entire worldviews.

To the Romantic poets and historians of the 19th and 20th centuries, Malinche’s life offered an irresistible archetype. She was portrayed not simply as a political figure, but as a tragic heroine caught in an impossible storm of destiny. The bond between the Spanish captain and his Indigenous interpreter took on the quality of a grand, doomed romance—a complex union of intimacy and conflict that ultimately gave birth to the *mestizo* identity, a new people born of two colliding worlds. In this Romantic light, her story is one of profound vulnerability and strength: a woman navigating the ultimate act of survival through love, intellect, and translation.

Over time, however, her name evolved into something broader. The term **"Malinches"** came to represent more than just one historical woman; it became a symbol for those caught between competing worlds, identities, and loyalties. While modern critiques sometimes unfairly reduced her to a figure of betrayal—coining the term *malinchismo*—a contemporary and romantic reevaluation views these "Malinches" differently. They are seen as pioneers of hybridity, women of immense emotional and intellectual power who held the keys to communication when empires fought for dominance.

Ultimately, the myth of La Malinche endures because it touches upon universal Romantic themes: the power of language to bridge vast divides, the bittersweet nature of intense love amidst war, and the indelible marks left when two different worlds forever intertwine. In the tapestry of Spanish history and literature, her legacy remains a haunting, beautiful ballad of passion, transformation, and rebirth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 3-part prose poem set in the American Southwest starting in 1996. Explore themes of intimacy, surveillance, colonialism, and borderlands using imagery of target practice, cartography, Spanish phrases, and references to Malinche and Circe.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. 1996: The Optics of the Grid**

In 1996, the desert greens only under the phosphor glow of early night-vision, a fluorescent smear across the Sonoran dark. We drive out past the dry wash where the caliche hardens like bone, carrying paper silhouettes stapled to saguaro ribs—human shapes with black bullseyes printed where the chest should open. You press your shoulder against mine to steady my aim, your thumb tracing the meridian of my jawline like a surveyor fixing a benchmark. *Mira through the glass,* you whisper, your breath smelling of metallic dust and crushed creosote. Through the crosshairs, the landscape is flattened into grid lines: latitude 31°20'N, a clean mathematical execution of territory. Behind us on the ridge, the remote tower hums, its infrared eyes sweeping the border scrub for heat signatures, blurring the warmth of migrating bodies with the warmth of jackrabbits. I think of Malinche, her tongue caught between two colliding empires, translating her own unmaking into the language of the conqueror. To speak here is to hand over the coordinates; to hold the rifle steady is to accept the map drawn by someone else’s boots. *El ojo que todo lo ve* blinks on its mast, calculating distance, windage, and the quiet, treasonous rhythm of our breathing.


**II. Aeaea in the Scrubland**

We make an island out of this arid stretch, an Aeaea bounded not by salt water but by ironwood and rusted barbed wire. In the midday glare, intimacy becomes an act of occupation: I trace the topographical contours of your spine with an unsharpened pencil, marking the dip of your lower back as a disputed valley, the rise of your hip as a boundary line waiting to be redrawn. We drink moonshine distilled from wild agave, our voices thick and slow in the heat, caught in Circe’s yard among the spent brass casings and sun-bleached skulls. Here, colonialism is not an ancient shadow; it is the land grant buried in the county vault, the line that splits a river in two and names one side *patria* and the other *nada*. You pull me down into the shade of the tailgate, your hands heavy with the memory of target practice, claiming the soft flesh beneath my ribs. *¿A quién le pertenece este cuerpo?* you ask into the hollow of my throat. Circe knew the secret of transformation was simple isolation: strip a man of his city, enclose him in scrubland, and watch him turn to beast or shadow. Over our heads, a Border Patrol helicopter chops the sky into violent fragments, its searchlight dragging a circle of white fire through the dark, hunting for anything that refuses to stay mapped.


**III. The Recoil and the Un-Mapping**

Years later, the paper targets from 1996 have dissolved into the dust, but the bullets remain, swallowed by the roots of brittlebush. Surveillance has shed its wires and grown seamless; overhead, silent drones track the heat of our ghosts, rendering our private history as a cluster of red pixels on a monitor in a air-conditioned room miles away. We stand at the border wall where the bollards slice the horizon into uniform vertical bars, a iron cage driven deep into the earth's ancient skin. I pick up a rusted shell casing, cold and hollow, and hold it to my ear like a seashell from Circe’s forgotten coast. In its empty chamber, I hear Malintzin’s voice, untranslated and fierce, rising above the hum of the high-voltage fences. *Dispara,* the desert whispers through the chain-link, *dispara y habla.* To inhabit this borderland is to be simultaneously the sniper and the target, the cartographer’s ink and the mountain that erases the line. We unfold the old paper map across the hood of the truck, but the desert wind takes it, tearing latitudinal lines from longitudinal seams, scattering our coordinates into the dust until there is no empire left to claim us—only the unmonitored, burning light of the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**TRIANGULATION: MONSOON, 1996**

In July of 1996, the border was a green hum  
inside a Sony Trinitron monitor.  
Outside, the dust of the Punjab plain smelled of wet copper,  
and my aunt stood under a forty-watt bulb at the check-post,  
her *dupatta* pinned at the shoulder with a rusted safety pin.  

On the desk: a brass ruler, an atlas bound in pigskin,  
and a computer that whined like a trapped cicada  
as it dialed the district office in Lahore.  
The guard was nineteen, carrying a Chinese-made rifle,  
his eyes sliding over her body the way his pencil  
traced the blue artery of the Ravi River—  
a line drawn in London sixty years prior  
by a man who had never felt this heat,  
a man who mistook a seasonal flood  
for a permanent edge.

*i. Cartography*  

They taught us that maps are objective.  
They taught us that Mercator was a saint of geometry,  
smoothing the curve of the earth  
so white ships could find their way to our spices.  
But a map is only a deed of theft  
rendered in watercolor.  

To grid a land is to domesticate it.  
To name a ridge is to claim its timber.  

*Latitude 31°32’ N, Longitude 74°20’ E.*  
The state calls this a coordinate.  
My grandmother called it the field where the mustard died  
when the fence went up and cut the well in half.

*ii. The Gaze*  

In 1996, surveillance was still analog enough to smell like warm dust,  
yet digital enough to turn a woman into a row of binary code.  
The guard logged her age: *34*.  
Her status: *Unaccompanied*.  
In the ledger of the state, an unaccompanied woman  
is an unmapped territory—  
a temptation to the surveyor’s stake,  
an open frontier requiring governance.  

He made her untie her hair.  
Search for hidden notes, he claimed.  
Search for contraband.  

I watched from the backseat of the Maruti Suzuki,  
ten years old, my knees pressed against vinyl seats,  
learning the grammar of the border:  
that to be female and native  
is to be constantly searched for a border breach  
you didn't commit.  

His gaze was not merely male;  
it was imperial.  
It was the land-surveyor’s lens,  
the census taker’s ink,  
the satellite that swooped over our fields that summer,  
taking infrared photographs  
to prove our soil belonged to the bank.

*iii. The Body as Unsovereign Ground*  

They map the land so they can march across it.  
They map our bodies so they can regulate the yield.  

* [Redacted: The length of her waist]  
* [Redacted: The language spoken in her throat]  
* [Redacted: The three generations of women who crossed this river before the line existed]  

He stamped her paper with a purple die.  
The ink bled through to the other side of the page,  
staining her thumb.  
*Permitted to pass.*  
As if the ground belonged to his uniform.  
As if the river required his thumbprint to flow south.

*iv. 1996 / 2026*  

Now, thirty years later, the cameras are smaller.  
They sit on poles like iron crows,  
using facial recognition to measure the angle of a woman’s jaw  
as she marches against the new dams.  

The maps are interactive now, rendered in sleek vector tiles,  
yet the logic remains unchanged:  
*Divide. Scale. Possess.*  

But I remember the rain in 1996,  
how it washed the chalk line off the asphalt before the guard could finish his shift.  
How the mud he tried to measure  
clung to my aunt’s feet—  
un-gridded,  
un-governed,  
carrying the dirt of three unmapped empires  
past his watchtower,  
into the dark.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem in three numbered sections about a complex, power-skewed connection between two people in a desert borderland? I want it to feel sharp and evocative, touching on anthropology, mapping, exile, and reclaiming agency through language.
counterfactuals.output:
**I.**

He brought a brass theodolite to measure my shadow,
calling the dust *an ethnographic baseline*,
the salt flat *a clean slate*.
In his leather-bound field notes, I am recorded
as a specimen of the perimeter—
a creature of low-humidity endurance,
my lineage reduced to carbon, quarter-inches,
and the cadence of a dying dialect.
He rests a hand upon my shoulder not to hold,
but to anchor his tripod against the wind.
He owns the glass; I own the sun it bends.
He calls me *informant*, calls himself *observer*,
writing down the architecture of my thirst
as if the drought were a symptom
of my backwardness, and not his grid.


**II.**

The fence is a cold seam through a burning plain.
He draws the border in blue ink across my skin,
mapping latitude lines over the topography of my collarbone,
a surveyor claiming a kingdom of stones.
To be in exile here is not to be far from home,
but to be made a stranger inside your own skin—
trapped in the margin between his coordinates
and the ghost-rivers that only run in winter.
He trades me water for toponyms,
wants the names of plants that survive without rain,
the names of passages where the guards look away.
He thinks power is the right to chart the waste;
he does not see that the mirage is a strategy,
that the land dissolves every line he scratches into it.


**III.**

Tonight, while he sleeps beside his drafting table,
I take his graphite and chew it to a paste.
I spit the black marrow back onto the sand.
I am un-naming his maps.
I speak a syntax he cannot transcribe—
a language made of dry wind, quartz-grit, and refusal.
Where he wrote *Territory*, I say *Tongue*.
Where he wrote *Barren*, I say *Artery*.
Let his lexicons rot in their pigskin covers;
he cannot annex a horizon he cannot pronounce.
I reclaim the perimeter with my own mouth,
placing my native verbs like landmines along his grid,
until the desert is no longer his study,
and I am no longer his subject,
and the border is just a line of dust
I blow away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
